title: What hazardous waste training does EPA require for large quantity generators?
description: What 40 CFR 262.17(a)(7) and 265.16 require: training within six months, an annual review, four document sets, and records kept until closure.
shortAnswer: Under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA), the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) requires large quantity generators to train facility personnel under 40 CFR 262.17(a)(7). Training must be completed within six months of hire or reassignment, be directed by a person trained in hazardous waste management, cover emergency response, and be followed by an annual review. Records on current staff are kept until facility closure and on former staff for three years.
keyTakeaways: Large quantity generators (1,000 kilograms or more of hazardous waste a month, or more than 1 kilogram of acute hazardous waste) must run a personnel training program under 40 CFR 262.17(a)(7) as a condition of accumulating waste without a permit.
Personnel must complete training within six months of employment, assignment to the facility, or a move to a new position, and must not work unsupervised until they do.
Training must be directed by a person trained in hazardous waste management procedures and must cover contingency plan implementation and six named emergency topics where applicable.
Every trained person takes part in an annual review of the initial training.

The facility keeps four document sets: job titles with names, written job descriptions, a written description of introductory and continuing training, and completion records, kept until closure for current staff and three years for former staff.
jurisdiction: United States (federal): 40 CFR Parts 262 and 265, plus authorized state programs
regulator: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and authorized state environmental agencies
appliesTo: Large quantity generators accumulating hazardous waste on site under 40 CFR 262.17
Owners and operators of interim status treatment, storage and disposal facilities under 40 CFR Part 265
Facility personnel whose positions relate to hazardous waste management, including handlers, supervisors and emergency coordinators
Small quantity generators, which have a lighter familiarity duty under 40 CFR 262.16(b)(9)(iii)

sections.heading: Which hazardous waste generators must run a training program?

blocks.text: Large quantity generators (LQGs) must run a formal personnel training program; small quantity generators have a lighter familiarity duty, and very small quantity generators have no federal training requirement. The generator category depends on the monthly quantity of hazardous waste generated at the site.

EPA's [generator categories page](https://www.epa.gov/hwgenerators/categories-hazardous-waste-generators) defines LQGs as sites that generate 1,000 kilograms or more of hazardous waste per month, or more than one kilogram per month of acutely hazardous waste. LQGs may generally accumulate waste on site for no more than 90 days. The training requirement sits inside [40 CFR 262.17](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-I/part-262/subpart-A/section-262.17), the conditions for exemption that let an LQG accumulate waste without a storage permit or interim status. Failing the training condition therefore puts the permit exemption itself at risk, not only a single paperwork rule.

blocks.text: Most states are authorized to run the RCRA program, and EPA notes that state generator categories and requirements can be different or more stringent than the federal rules. A multi-site program should map each site to its state rule before using the federal text as the baseline.

sections.heading: What must the LQG training program cover?

blocks.text: The program must teach personnel to perform their duties in a way that keeps the facility compliant with Part 262, and it must prepare them to respond effectively to emergencies. Section 262.17(a)(7)(i)(A) allows classroom instruction, online training (for example computer based or electronic) or on the job training.

Two design rules apply. The program must be directed by a person trained in hazardous waste management procedures, and it must include instruction on hazardous waste management procedures, including contingency plan implementation, relevant to the positions in which people are employed. At a minimum, it must familiarize personnel with emergency procedures, equipment and systems, including where applicable:

items: Procedures for using, inspecting, repairing and replacing facility emergency and monitoring equipment.
Key parameters for automatic waste feed cut off systems.

blocks.text: Section 262.17(a)(7)(i)(D) lets a facility avoid duplicating emergency response training for employees already trained under the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) emergency response rules at 29 CFR 1910.120(p)(8) and 1910.120(q), provided the overall facility training still meets every condition in the section. The OSHA side is covered on the [HAZWOPER training page](/regulations/osha-hazwoper-training-requirements).

sections.heading: How soon must training be completed, and how often is it repeated?

blocks.text: Facility personnel must complete the program within six months of employment, assignment to the facility, or assignment to a new position at the facility, whichever is later, and then take part in an annual review of the initial training. Until they complete it, they must not work in unsupervised positions.

The six month window is a ceiling, not a target. Because untrained staff cannot work unsupervised, a facility that relies on the full six months needs a documented supervision arrangement for every new or transferred person in the interim. The trigger also includes internal moves: a waste handler promoted to an accumulation area lead has a new position, so the clock restarts for the role specific content.

The rule says "annual review" without defining a format or length. Most programs treat it as a scheduled refresher that revisits the initial content, adds changes to the contingency plan and procedures, and records attendance. Setting the cycle is covered in [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What training records must an LQG keep, and for how long?

blocks.text: The LQG must keep four document sets at the facility, and training records on current personnel must be retained until closure of the facility, with records on former employees kept at least three years from the date the employee last worked there. Records may follow personnel transferred within the same company.

items: **Job titles and names:** the job title for each position related to hazardous waste management and the name of the employee filling it (262.17(a)(7)(iv)(A)).
**Job descriptions:** a written description of each listed position, including the requisite skill, education or other qualifications and the duties of personnel assigned to it (262.17(a)(7)(iv)(B)).
**Training description:** a written description of the type and amount of both introductory and continuing training given to each person filling a listed position (262.17(a)(7)(iv)(C)).
**Completion records:** records that the training or job experience required by the section has been given to, and completed by, facility personnel (262.17(a)(7)(iv)(D)).

blocks.title: Retention is tied to the facility, not the person
blocks.text: "Until closure of the facility" means a current employee's training history can never be purged on a fixed cycle while the site operates. A records schedule that deletes LMS completions after, say, seven years breaks this rule for long serving staff. See [how long to keep training records](/guides/how-long-to-keep-training-records).

sections.heading: How does the TSD facility rule in 40 CFR 265.16 compare, and what changed in 2016?

blocks.text: Interim status treatment, storage and disposal (TSD) facilities follow [40 CFR 265.16](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-I/part-265/subpart-B/section-265.16), which contains the same core structure: a program directed by a trained person, the six emergency topics, completion within six months, an annual review, the four document sets, and retention until closure or three years after an employee leaves.

The main textual difference is delivery method. Section 265.16(a)(1) refers to classroom instruction or on the job training, while 262.17(a)(7) expressly adds online training. The LQG version came from the Hazardous Waste Generator Improvements Rule, which EPA's [rule page](https://www.epa.gov/hwgenerators/final-rule-hazardous-waste-generator-improvements) says was signed on October 28, 2016, published on November 28, 2016, and effective May 30, 2017. Before that rule, LQGs reached the Part 265 training standard by cross reference.

EPA has since made technical corrections to the generator rules. Its rule page records that five amendments finalized on December 11, 2024 had their effective date delayed to March 21, 2025. As at November 2026 the training paragraph in 262.17(a)(7) reads as quoted on this page, but state adoption of federal amendments runs on each state's own timetable.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models each hazardous waste position, its written job description and its required training as linked objects, so the four RCRA document sets come from one source rather than four spreadsheets. Emergency topics are tied to the current contingency plan version, which shows which annual review content must change when the plan changes.

faqs.q: Can RCRA training for large quantity generators be delivered online?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 262.17(a)(7)(i)(A) expressly allows classroom instruction, online training such as computer based or electronic courses, or on the job training. The program must still be directed by a person trained in hazardous waste management procedures and must be relevant to each person's position, so a generic online course alone rarely satisfies the rule.

faqs.q: Does the RCRA rule set a minimum number of training hours?
faqs.a: No. Neither 262.17(a)(7) nor 265.16 sets hours. Instead, the facility must keep a written description of the type and amount of introductory and continuing training for each position, so the facility sets the amount and must then deliver what it wrote down. Inspectors compare that description with the completion records.

faqs.q: Do small quantity generators need a written training program?
faqs.a: Not under federal rules. Section 262.16(b)(9)(iii) requires a small quantity generator to ensure all employees are thoroughly familiar with proper waste handling and emergency procedures relevant to their responsibilities. EPA describes this as basic training. Some authorized states impose more, so the state rule should be checked.

faqs.q: Is OSHA HAZWOPER training the same as RCRA training?
faqs.a: They overlap but are separate obligations. RCRA training protects compliance and emergency response at the facility; HAZWOPER under 29 CFR 1910.120 protects worker safety. The RCRA rule lets a facility count OSHA emergency response training under 1910.120(p)(8) and (q) toward its emergency content, provided the overall program still meets every RCRA condition.
